analysis.one_liner: Lets gig companies give workers COVID-era benefits without those benefits counting as evidence the workers are employees.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or vote; it died in the House Education and Labor Committee when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: During the COVID-19 emergency, gig platforms like ride and delivery apps could have given workers cash help, health benefits, protective equipment, and health checks. Normally, a company doing those things can be cited as evidence that its workers are really employees. This bill would have made that impossible under any federal, state, or local law through the end of the emergency period, shielding the platforms' contractor-based business model while workers got temporary help.
analysis.who_benefits: Gig platform companies gain the most: any benefits or safety measures they provided during the emergency could not be used as evidence that their workers are employees or that the company is a joint employer. That protects the contractor model that keeps platforms from owing minimum wage, overtime, unemployment insurance, and collective bargaining rights. Gig workers would get some temporary COVID-era assistance — cash help when they couldn't work, health benefits, protective gear, and testing — but only in a form that doesn't change their legal status.

how_it_helps.text: During the COVID-19 emergency period, digital marketplace companies could provide financial assistance to workers who couldn't work due to health or safety concerns, health-related benefits, safety training, medical and cleaning supplies, health checks, and medical testing.
None of those actions could be used under any federal, state, or local law as evidence that a worker is an employee or independent contractor, or that the company is a joint employer.
The protection ran from March 15, 2020 to the later of June 30, 2021 or the end of the federal COVID-19 public health emergency.

analysis.who_pays: Gig workers pay in legal rights: while the safe harbor was in effect, the very conduct that signals employment — a company directing your work, paying your health costs, supplying your equipment — could no longer be raised in any court or agency as evidence that they are employees entitled to minimum wage, overtime, unemployment insurance, or other job protections.
analysis.who_pays_short: Gig workers trading away classification claims

drawbacks.text: The bill's central effect was to strip workers of evidence. When a company controls the work and pays for health care, that is normally what courts look at in deciding whether someone is an employee; the bill barred that line of reasoning under any law during the covered period.

Gig workers would remain outside the employment system — no guaranteed minimum wage, overtime, unemployment insurance, or right to organize — even while the platform directs their work and profits from it.

The bill was not a comprehensive gig-worker policy; it created a one-way legal shield for platforms during an emergency, with no offsetting guarantee of benefits, portable accounts, or minimum earnings for workers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The temporary help for gig workers during a pandemic is real but modest, and it comes attached to a significant legal giveaway: the bill would have made it harder to ever prove these workers are employees. An honest supporter would have to acknowledge that the bill's main work is protecting the contractor model, not delivering aid — aid platforms could have provided anyway, at the cost of a court case, before this bill existed.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee the day it was introduced, never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote, and expired when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Carol Miller (R-WV) introduced the bill on May 22, 2020, joined by original cosponsors including Reps. Cuellar, Balderson, Mooney, and Woodall.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor.
No further action was ever taken — no hearing, no markup, no vote.
The bill died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because it died, gig workers kept their existing ability to use platform conduct as evidence in employment-classification cases, and the platforms got no new legal shield. Nothing changed for anyone; the bill's main beneficiaries had it been enacted — the platforms — simply remain where they were.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Workers kept classification rights; platforms gained nothing

for.name: Rep. Carol Miller
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited cosponsors.

for.name: 1 of 231 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: The bill's only Democratic cosponsor signed on.

against.name: Rep. Bobby Scott
against.role: Chair, House Education and Labor Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill; it sat untouched in committee until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Of the bill's 10 cosponsors, 9 were Republicans and 1 was a Democrat, and the committee chaired by a Democrat took no action on it.

industries.industry: Gig platform companies (rideshare, food delivery, home-sharing apps)
industries.note: The bill would have let platforms supply COVID-era benefits and safety measures while barring those actions from counting as evidence of employment or joint-employer status under any law. That locks in the contractor model that keeps workers outside minimum wage, overtime, and unemployment insurance — the platform's gain is precisely the workers' lost claim.
